UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Southern Indiana Gas and Electric Company              )
                                                       )
           v.                                          )         Docket No. EL26-38-000
                                                       )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.         )

                                 COMMENTS OF
            THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI

           Pursuant to Rule 206 1 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC) and the Commission’s Notice of Filing issued

January 6, 2026, the Public Service Commission of the State of Missouri (Missouri PSC) submits

the following comments in response to a complaint by Southern Indiana Gas and Electric

Company d/b/a CenterPoint Energy Indiana South (SIGE) against the Midcontinent Independent

System Operator, Inc. (MISO) in this docket.



                                   I. Service and Communication

           All pleadings, correspondence and other communications related to this proceeding

should be directed to:

                                              II. Background

         The Public Service Commission of the State of Missouri (Missouri PSC) is a “state

commission” as defined in Section 1.101(k) of the Commission’s Rules of General

Applicability. 2 The Missouri PSC regulates rates, charges and terms of service for the sale and

distribution of electricity by public utilities to consumers in the state, under a traditional

vertically integrated regulatory structure. 3 Missouri law requires public utilities under the

jurisdiction of the Missouri PSC to provide service to their customers that is “safe and adequate

and in all respects just and reasonable.” 4 The Missouri PSC has approved electrical corporations

under its jurisdiction to be members of two Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs): the

Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (MISO) and the Southwest Power Pool, Inc.

(SPP).

         In its complaint, SIGE requests a Commission order directing MISO to revise its Open

Access Transmission, Energy, and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff (Tariff) to provide a cost

recovery and allocation mechanism for SIGE to recover all costs, net of market revenues,

associated with a recent order (DOE Order) from the U.S. Secretary of Energy (Secretary). 5 In

the DOE Order, the Secretary determined that the continued operation of SIGE’s F.B. Culley

Generating Station Unit 2 (Culley Unit) beyond its planned retirement date “is necessary to best

meet the emergency arising from increased demand, determined shortage, and other causes, and

serve the public interest under FPA section 202(c).” 6

                                        III. Summary of Comments

        The Secretary’s continued use of FPA Section 202(c) to keep power plants operating past

their planned retirement date raises important questions for state commissions, which

traditionally oversee plant retirements. In these comments, the Missouri PSC reiterates the need

for FERC to direct MISO to convene a stakeholder process to develop a tariff to address 202(c)

orders. The Missouri PSC also urges FERC to require SIGE and other owners of plants subject to

202(c) orders to provide regular reports on the costs of compliance. The Missouri PSC

appreciates the opportunity to comment on this complaint. 7



                                  IV. Comments of the Missouri PSC

A.      The continued use of Section 202(c) orders provides new justification for

stakeholder involvement in cost allocation.

        This case follows the template set by Consumers Energy in FERC Docket No. EL25-90.

In that case, the Organization of MISO States, Inc. (OMS) and the Missouri PSC asked the

Commission to establish a stakeholder process to produce a tariff that could address 202(c)

orders, on the grounds that such orders implicate state interests and were likely to continue. 8 But

the Commission decided that further process was not necessary, because “the most reasonable

reading of the DOE Order’s intended scope is that the emergency necessitating the continued

operation of the Campbell Plant is in Local Resource Zones 1-7.” 9 This reasoning no longer

applies, however, as this DOE Order finds an “emergency situation” in MISO more broadly,

No. 20250915-5160, pg. 2.
9
  FERC Docket No. EL25-90-000, Order On Complaint, 192 FERC ¶ 61,158, P. 41 (August 15, 2025).

                                                        3
 based upon “resource adequacy concerns” in MISO as a whole that go beyond the near term. 10

For example, the DOE Order relied on the 2025 OMS-MISO survey that includes resource

adequacy projections extending into 2031. 11 Although the OMS-MISO survey forecasts a

capacity surplus in MISO ranging from 1.4 GW to 6.1 GW for summer 2026, 12 the DOE Order

purports to address a “potential longer term resource adequacy emergency in MISO.” 13 These

issues pertain to all of MISO. This DOE Order makes only passing reference to Local Resource

Zones 1-7, so the reasonableness of reflexively allocating the costs of this order to Zones 1-7 on

a load ratio share basis is no longer self-evident.

       This DOE Order broadens its definition of “emergency” to encompass longer-term

resource planning issues and therefore encroaches further into state resource adequacy

jurisdiction. This more expansive DOE Order justifies a more comprehensive approach at MISO,

one involving the state commissions that represent the consumers who will pay to keep these

plants operating, while also paying for the capacity planned to replace them. The Commission

should acknowledge the fact that the DOE’s 202(c) orders are not “one-offs.” Their expanded

use implicates state resource planning. The Commission should direct MISO to initiate a

stakeholder process and develop a tariff to meet that reality.

 B.      Stakeholders and consumers are entitled to more transparency about the ongoing

use and costs of the DOE’s 202(c) orders.

        The transparency of the costs imposed on consumers falls squarely within the issue of

cost allocation that the DOE has delegated to FERC under its 202(c) orders. 14 Under the Federal

Power Act and state law, state commissions like the Missouri PSC retain authority to decide

what amount and what type of resources constitute safe and adequate service, and how much

retail customers in their jurisdictions should pay for that service. 15 As the DOE expands the use

and scope of 202(c) orders to encompass more issues of state-jurisdictional resource planning,

the Commission should use its cost allocation authority to ensure that state planners and

consumers in MISO have timely information about the costs and benefits of 202(c) orders.

        Commission precedent supports transparency requirements when resources are used

outside normal operations. For example, in 2006 the Commission approved “Exceptional

Dispatch” provisions to authorize the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) to

manually commit and/or dispatch resources in order to maintain reliable grid operations under

unusual and infrequent circumstances. 16 The Commission ordered CAISO to make reports every

60 days detailing the “frequency, volume, costs, causes and degree of mitigation of exceptional

dispatches.” 17 The Commission found that regular reporting would “provide the necessary

transparency to enable stakeholders to remain informed about the use of Exceptional Dispatch…

.” 18 The Commission further found that frequent, transparent reporting “should help facilitate

 any stakeholder processes concerning the development of additional market mechanisms to

address situations that frequently give rise to exceptional dispatches.” 19

           Similarly, additional transparency about the use and costs of plants subject to 202(c)

emergency orders will help MISO stakeholders better understand how such orders mitigate

resource adequacy concerns. As the DOE Order notes, MISO and its stakeholders have

implemented new tariff provisions, like the Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS), to

address reliability needs. 20 More transparency about the costs and benefits of

202(c) orders will help MISO and its stakeholders evaluate new approaches to reliability, and

will be of particular benefit to state commissions as they evaluate the retirement of power plants

within their jurisdictions. On this basis, FERC should direct SIGE and other owners of plants

subject to 202(c) orders to submit regular reports into these cost allocation dockets about the

plants’ continued operations and their costs, subject to appropriate confidentiality provisions.



                                             V. Conclusion

           The Missouri PSC respectfully submits these comments.
